extracted.intended_audience: The people/citizens of New York; voters deciding on ratification of the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th‑century political essay arguing for adoption of the proposed U.S. Constitution, addressing objections about bills of rights, liberty of the press, expense, representation, and amendability, and giving guidance on what constitutes adequate constitutional protections and practical procedure. Intended to persuade citizens to ratify now and pursue amendments later if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habeas corpus and prohibition of ex post facto laws as securities to liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The establishment of the writ of habeas corpus, the prohibition of ex post facto laws, and of titles of nobility are perhaps greater securities to liberty and republicanism than any [other] provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These protections guard against arbitrary imprisonments and retroactive penal legislation; Blackstone calls the habeas corpus act 'the BULWARK of the British Constitution.' The text emphasizes these as fundamental safeguards against despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of titles of nobility as a cornerstone of republican government
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing need be said to illustrate the importance of the prohibition of titles of nobility. This may truly be denominated the corner-stone of republican government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding titles helps ensure the government remains that of the people and prevents aristocratic concentrations of power; it is singled out as a primary structural protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bills of rights unnecessary and potentially dangerous in a people-founded constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills of rights, in the sense and to the extent contended for, are not only unnecessary in the proposed Constitution, but would even be dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bill of rights could contain exceptions to powers not granted and thereby furnish a pretext ('a colorable pretext') for claiming more power by constructive implication. In a constitution founded on popular sovereignty, the people surrender nothing, so specific reservations are unnecessary and may be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations of rights (e.g., liberty of the press) are indeterminate and rely on public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: What signifies a declaration, that 'the liberty of the press shall be inviolably preserved'? What is the liberty of the press? Who can give it any definition which would not leave the utmost latitude for evasion? I hold it to be impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Security for freedoms like the press depends fundamentally on public opinion and the spirit of the people and government, not on fine constitutional declarations whose terms are vague and easily evaded; practical society and sentiment are the real guarantors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of common and state law under the Constitution (subject to legislative alteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pretended establishment of the common and state law by the Constitution... they are expressly made subject 'to such alterations and provisions as the legislature shall from time to time make concerning the same.' They are at any moment liable to repeal by the ordinary legislative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A declaration that recognizes ancient law only removes doubts; it does not constitutionalize those laws or place them beyond ordinary legislative control.

rubrics_metrics.name: The proposed Constitution itself functions as a bill of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution is itself, in every rational sense, and to every useful purpose, A BILL OF RIGHTS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plan of the convention contains ample and precise provisions defining political privileges and many immunities and modes of proceeding relative to personal and private concerns; the placement/order of declarations is immaterial if substantive protections exist anywhere in the instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance of the seat of government does not preclude accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to confer such large powers upon the national government, because the seat of that government must of necessity be too remote... This argument is not well founded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People gain information about representatives through public prints, correspondence, and intelligent intermediaries; state governments act as sentinels over national officers and can communicate knowledge to constituents, so distance is not a decisive impediment to oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union restrains local factions and secures republic, liberty, and property
rubrics_metrics.description: The additional securities to republican government, to liberty and to property... consist chiefly in the restraints which the preservation of the Union will impose on local factions and insurrections, and on the ambition of powerful individuals in single States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union diminishes opportunities for foreign intrigue, prevents extensive standing militaries born of inter-state wars, guarantees republican government, excludes titles of nobility, and guards against State practices that undermine property and credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections about debts to the United States are groundless; changes in government do not discharge obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The suggestion that the proposed Constitution tacitly relinquishes debts due to the United States is entirely void of foundation... 'States neither lose any of their rights, nor are discharged from any of their obligations, by a change in the form of their civil government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that omission of a provision respecting debts implies abandonment are dismissed as ignorance or dishonesty; established political law maintains continuity of obligations despite changes in governmental form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expense of the new government is not a decisive objection—savings offset extra costs
rubrics_metrics.description: If it were even true, that the adoption of the proposed government would occasion a considerable increase of expense, it would be an objection that ought to have no weight against the plan... The sources of additional expense are much fewer than may have been imagined; they are counterbalanced by considerable objects of saving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both added costs (e.g., judges' support, revenue collection officers) and savings (shorter sessions of national and state legislatures, consolidation of functions). The balance may favor the Union and a less expensive government could be incompetent to the purposes of the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication of federal offices is largely an exchange, not an addition, of personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons to be employed in the collection of the revenues will be wholly of the national description. The States individually will stand in no need of any for this purpose... It will be in most cases nothing more than an exchange of State for national officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The number or salaries of national officers should not be presumed to exceed those previously paid by states; many roles will transfer rather than multiply, so projected expense increases from this source are questionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support of judges is an extra expense but not materially consequential
rubrics_metrics.description: The support of the judges will clearly be an extra expense, but to what extent will depend on the particular plan... upon no reasonable plan can it amount to a sum which will be an object of material consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge judiciary costs but weigh them against greater efficiency and security benefits; they are not fatal to the plan's adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization will save time and expense by reducing state legislatures' burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of the United States has hitherto occupied the State legislatures... Now the members who compose the legislatures of the several States amount to two thousand and upwards, which number has hitherto performed what under the new system will be done... by sixty-five persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By transferring national business to a central Congress and executive, state legislators will have shorter sessions and attend only to state affairs, producing economies in time and expense that offset national costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt now and amend later—subsequent amendments are easier to achieve
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be far more easy to obtain subsequent than previous amendments to the Constitution... If the Constitution proposed should once be ratified by all the States as it stands, alterations in it may at any time be effected by nine States. Here, then, the chances are as thirteen to nine in favor of subsequent amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because amendments can be proposed and ratified more feasibly after adoption (per the plan's Article V mechanism), it is more practical to accept an imperfect but workable constitution and rely on the amendatory process than to demand perfection before establishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection in a constitution is unattainable; experience and time will correct defects
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgments of many must unite in the work; EXPERIENCE must guide their labor; TIME must bring it to perfection, and the FEELING of inconveniences must correct the mistakes which they inevitably fall into in their first trials and experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political prudence favors adopting a functioning system now rather than risking anarchy by pursuing an idealized perfect plan—amendment and gradual correction are realistic paths to improvement.
